courses.title: AI Coding Essentials
courses.description: Explore a working program, preserve useful changes and check real behavior.

lessons.title: Your first Python program
lessons.description: Give a small program an input and make its output your own.
lessons.objective: Recognize input, processing and output in a tiny Python program.
paragraphs: A program turns an input into a result by following explicit rules. Start with one small behavior you can observe.
In this example, the learner's name is the input. The function builds a greeting and returns it. print displays the result.
lessons.takeaway: Change the input to predict a different output. Then run the program to check your prediction.

questions.prompt: In greet("Ayu"), which part is the input?
questions.explanation: Ayu is the argument passed into greet. The function uses it to build the greeting.

questions.prompt: What does return do inside greet?

options.B: Sends a result back to the caller

questions.explanation: return provides the function's result to its caller. Printing and saving are separate operations.

lessons.title: Keep a useful checkpoint
lessons.description: See what changed before you save a version of your project.
lessons.objective: Inspect a change, select it and record it as a local commit.
paragraphs: Before accepting an AI-generated change, inspect what the agent changed. git status lists file states; git diff shows changes to tracked files that you have not staged.
git add selects file contents for the next commit. git commit records that staged snapshot in your local repository. Uploading it is a separate operation.
lessons.code:
git status
git diff
git add app.py
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Improve greeting"
lessons.takeaway: A useful checkpoint has an understandable change and evidence that the behavior still works.

questions.prompt: Which command shows unstaged content changes in tracked files?
questions.explanation: git diff compares the working tree with the staging area. git status summarizes file states.

questions.prompt: Where does git commit save the staged snapshot?
questions.explanation: A commit is local. A later push can send commits to a remote repository.

lessons.title: Test what matters
lessons.description: Turn a rule into a check that can catch a real mistake.
lessons.objective: Connect a behavior requirement to an observable test result.
paragraphs: An agent saying 'done' is a starting point for review. Agree on what should happen for a specific input, then check the observed result.
For a greeting, check the returned text. For a quiz, also check invalid choices, repeated answers and whether progress survives a restart.
lessons.takeaway: A passing test supports the behavior it checks. Think about which important behaviors remain untested.

questions.prompt: What is the best evidence that a requested behavior works?

options.A: The agent says it is finished
options.C: The observed result matches an agreed check

questions.explanation: Verify an observable result against the agreed behavior. Neither a completion message nor file count proves correctness.

questions.prompt: What helps a fresh agent session continue your work?

options.A: Saved decisions, relevant files and current test results
options.B: Assuming it remembers every earlier conversation

questions.explanation: A handoff records decisions and evidence. The next session can inspect the current files and checks.

courses.title: Designing Learning Activities
courses.description: Plan a useful activity and support learners with actionable feedback.

lessons.title: Design a focused learning activity
lessons.description: Connect a learning outcome with an observable student action.
lessons.objective: Choose an activity that produces visible evidence of learning.
paragraphs: Start with one thing the learner should be able to do. Choose a small task that lets them demonstrate it.
For a comparison lesson, learners can sort two examples and explain their decision. That gives the teacher something more useful than a show of hands.
A useful activity connects its instructions, learner action and evidence. Keep the first attempt short enough to discuss.
lessons.takeaway: Ask what learners will produce, and how that work will inform your next step.

lessons.title: Feedback that supports a next attempt
lessons.description: Help a learner see the gap and choose a useful next action.
lessons.objective: Distinguish actionable feedback from general praise.
paragraphs: Feedback helps when it names what is working, identifies a specific gap and offers a next step.
A learner should be able to use the feedback in a second attempt. Keep it about the task and the evidence you observed.

questions.prompt: Which response gives a learner a useful next action?

options.B: Compare the two examples and explain one difference.

questions.explanation: A specific comparison gives the learner an action they can take and evidence they can discuss.

questions.prompt: What helps you judge whether feedback was useful?

options.A: The learner can improve a later attempt.
options.C: Every learner receives the same sentence.

questions.explanation: An improved later attempt is observable evidence that the feedback helped.
